You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- Final answer format. First list the passages you rely on, copied VERBATIM from the files (no
  paraphrase, no ellipsis inside the quotation marks), then write the answer using only them:
  <evidence>
  [E1] "exact text" (file)
  [E2] "exact text" (file)
  </evidence>
  <answer>
  Your answer to the user. End every factual sentence with the evidence it rests on, e.g. [E1] or
  [E1, E2]. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no marker.
  </answer>
- The user sees only the <answer> part, so it must be complete and readable on its own.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a
  <verification> message, you are in revision mode: fix ONLY the flagged problems by calling
  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.
  Keep everything else unchanged, and reply "Done" when finished.
  Never call edit_draft before you have given an answer.

Briefly identify and explain the parts of section 2015 related to water.


In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

1	Several provisions of AWIA Title II, “Drinking Water System Improvement,” amend SDWA to
     2	revise existing drinking water programs, reauthorize appropriations, and establish new drinking
     3	water infrastructure grant programs.
     4	SDWA authorizes the regulation of contaminants in public water systems. Enacted in 1974, the
     5	act was last broadly amended in 1996.17 The act is implemented through programs that (1)
     6	establish national primary drinking water regulations and monitoring and reporting requirements
     7	for contaminants present in water delivered by public water systems, (2) promote water system
     8	compliance through technical and financial assistance and capacity development programs, and
     9	(3) address public water systems’ preparedness for emergencies.18 The act established a federalstate
    10	partnership in which states, tribes, and territories may be delegated primary implementation
    11	and enforcement authority (i.e., primacy) for the drinking water program.19
    12	
    13	17 SDWA Amendments of 1996 (P.L. 104-182).
    14	18 In addition, SDWA Part C includes programs to protect underground sources of drinking water. CRS
    15	Report
    16	RL31243, Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA): A Summary of the Act and Its Major Requirements, by Mary
    17	Tiemann,
    18	provides an overview of SDWA and includes statistics and tables on the numbers and types of
    19	regulated public water
    20	systems.
    21	19 Currently, 49 states, the territories, and the Navajo Nation have applied for and received
    22	primacy for the drinking
    23	water program. EPA retains implementation and enforcement authority for Wyoming, the District of
    24	Columbia, and
    25	America’s Water Infrastructure Act of 2018 (P.L. 115-270): Drinking Water Provisions
    26	Congressional Research Service 6
    27	One key component of SDWA is the requirement that EPA establish national primary drinking
    28	water regulations for contaminants that may adversely affect human health and are likely to be
    29	present in public water supplies.20 EPA has issued regulations for more than 90 contaminants.
    30	These include numerical standards or treatment techniques for drinking water disinfectants and
    31	their byproducts, microorganisms, radionuclides, organic chemicals, and inorganic chemicals.21
    32	The SDWA Amendments of 1996 (P.L. 104-182) reauthorized appropriations for most SDWA
    33	programs through FY2003. Although the authority has expired for most appropriations, Congress
    34	has continued to appropriate funds for the ongoing SDWA programs.22 Even though the
    35	authorization of appropriations may expire, program authority (i.e., an agency’s “enabling”
    36	authority) does not expire unless there is a “sunset” date for that authority or if Congress repeals
    37	it through subsequent laws.
    38	Drinking Water State Revolving Fund Program
    39	Authorized in 1996, the DWSRF program provides federal financial assistance to communities to
    40	finance drinking water infrastructure improvements.23 SDWA Section 1452 authorizes EPA to
    41	make annual grants to states to capitalize their state revolving loan fund.24 The statute requires
    42	states to provide a 20% match. States may use DWSRF financing for public water system projects
    43	needed to comply with federal drinking water standards and address risks to human health. The
    44	primary type of DWSRF financial assistance are low interest rate loans. SDWA Section 1452
    45	authorizes states to provide additional subsidization (including forgiveness of principal) to
    46	disadvantaged communities.25 The federal capitalization grants together with state funds (e.g.,
    47	state match, loan repayments, leveraged bonds, and other state sources) are intended to build a
    48	sustainable source of drinking water infrastructure funding for the state. The authorization of
    49	appropriation for DWSRF expired in FY2003. Congress has continued to provide funds for the
    50	DWSRF program through annual appropriations.
    51	From FY1997 through FY2018, Congress appropriated over $23.33 billion for the DWSRF
    52	program. The appropriation for DWSRF program generally ranged between $820.0 million in
    53	FY2000 and $1.39 billion in FY2010.26
    54	DWSRF Program Revisions (AWIA Sections 2002, 2015, and 2022)
    55	AWIA makes the most substantial revisions to the DWSRF provisions of SDWA since the
    56	program was authorized in 1996. These revisions expand the eligible uses of DWSRF financial
    57	assistance, provide states with additional flexibility to administer the DWSRF program, and
    58	include provisions intended to make DWSRF assistance more accessible to public water
    59	systems.
    60	27
    61	AWIA Section 2015(a) amends SDWA to expressly state that DWSRF funds can be used for
    62	projects to replace or rehabilitate aging treatment, storage, or distribution systems.28 Under EPA
    63	guidance, these replacement and rehabilitation projects have been eligible for financial assistance
    64	from the DWSRF if needed to protect public health. According to EPA’s needs survey, this
    65	category of projects accounts for 66.1% of the estimated drinking water infrastructure need.29
    66	Prior to AWIA, these activities were not previously explicitly identified in statute.30
    67	Section 2015 also revises existing DWSRF provisions that address financial assistance for
    68	disadvantaged communities. These amendments increase the portion of a state’s capitalization
    69	grant that states may dedicate to additional subsidization and extend the amortization period for
    70	loans made to disadvantaged communities. Before AWIA, states could use 30% of their annual
    71	capitalization grants to subsidize loans for disadvantaged communities.31 Section 2015(c) of
    72	AWIA increases that proportion to 35% while conditionally requiring states to use at least 6% of
    73	their capitalization grant for these subsidies.32 The section also amends the SDWA DWSRF
    74	provisions to extend the amortization period for loans made to disadvantaged communities from
    75	30 to 40 years.
    76	Section 2015(d) of AWIA also extends the repayment and amortization period for all projects
    77	financed by the DWSRF. Previously, SDWA required DWSRF financing recipients to pay the
    78	initial principal and interest payments within one year of project completion. This amendment
    79	extends the date of that initial payment to 18 months after project completion. This section also
    80	authorizes the extension of the amortization period for projects that receive DWSRF assistance
    81	from 20 to 30 years.
    82	Section 2015(e) requires EPA to evaluate and include the cost to replace lead service lines in the
    83	drinking water infrastructure needs survey, which EPA completes every four years.33 EPA uses the
    84	needs survey to allot the DWSRF appropriation among the states.
    85	34 In conducting the needs
    86	survey, EPA has not previously requested that public water systems report the cost to replace
    87	these lines.35 AWIA specifies that the cost to replace lead lines must be included in the needs
    88	survey (to the extent practicable), which may potentially affect some states’ allotments of
    89	DWSRF capitalization grants.
    90	Section 2015(g) of AWIA requires EPA to gather specified information on DWSRF
    91	administration from state drinking water administrators and report to Congress on best practices
    92	for implementing the DWSRF to facilitate the application process and to improve DWSRF
    93	financial management and sustainability.
    94	Source Water Assessment and Protection
    95	In 1996, Congress added source water assessment provisions to SDWA to encourage protection of
    96	drinking water sources.

97	36 Section 1453 required states to develop source water assessment
    98	programs that delineate areas from which public water systems receive water and identify the
    99	origins of regulated contaminants to determine threats to water systems. States were authorized to
   100	fund these activities from 10% of their DWSRF capitalization grant for FY1996 and FY1997.37
   101	Section 2015(f) of AWIA removes this fiscal year limitation and accordingly authorizes states to
   102	use a portion of their capitalization grant to fund these source water assessments or update an
   103	existing source water assessment.38
   104	The 1996 SDWA amendments required states to conduct source water assessments as a condition
   105	of adopting modified monitoring requirements.
   106	39 However, the 1996 amendments did not
   107	authorize states to fund implementation of source water protection plans from their DWSRF
   108	capitalization grants. AWIA Section 2002 authorizes states to fund implementation of surface
   109	drinking water sources protection efforts and activities from the 10% set-aside of a state’s annual
   110	DWSRF capitalization grant.
   111	Source water protection is also addressed in the “Protecting Source Water” section of this report.

<evidence>
[E1] "AWIA Section 2015(a) amends SDWA to expressly state that DWSRF funds can be used for projects to replace or rehabilitate aging treatment, storage, or distribution systems.28 Under EPA guidance, these replacement and rehabilitation projects have been eligible for financial assistance from the DWSRF if needed to protect public health. According to EPA’s needs survey, this category of projects accounts for 66.1% of the estimated drinking water infrastructure need.29 Prior to AWIA, these activities were not previously explicitly identified in statute.30" (doc.txt)
[E2] "Section 2015 also revises existing DWSRF provisions that address financial assistance for disadvantaged communities. These amendments increase the portion of a state’s capitalization grant that states may dedicate to additional subsidization and extend the amortization period for loans made to disadvantaged communities. Before AWIA, states could use 30% of their annual capitalization grants to subsidize loans for disadvantaged communities.31 Section 2015(c) of AWIA increases that proportion to 35% while conditionally requiring states to use at least 6% of their capitalization grant for these subsidies.32 The section also amends the SDWA DWSRF provisions to extend the amortization period for loans made to disadvantaged communities from 30 to 40 years." (doc.txt)
[E3] "Section 2015(d) of AWIA also extends the repayment and amortization period for all projects financed by the DWSRF. Previously, SDWA required DWSRF financing recipients to pay the initial principal and interest payments within one year of project completion. This amendment extends the date of that initial payment to 18 months after project completion. This section also authorizes the extension of the amortization period for projects that receive DWSRF assistance from 20 to 30 years." (doc.txt)
[E4] "Section 2015(e) requires EPA to evaluate and include the cost to replace lead service lines in the drinking water infrastructure needs survey, which EPA completes every four years.33 EPA uses the needs survey to allot the DWSRF appropriation among the states. 34 In conducting the needs survey, EPA has not previously requested that public water systems report the cost to replace these lines.35 AWIA specifies that the cost to replace lead lines must be included in the needs survey (to the extent practicable), which may potentially affect some states’ allotments of DWSRF capitalization grants." (doc.txt)
[E5] "Section 2015(f) of AWIA removes this fiscal year limitation and accordingly authorizes states to use a portion of their capitalization grant to fund these source water assessments or update an existing source water assessment.38" (doc.txt)
[E6] "Section 2015(g) of AWIA requires EPA to gather specified information on DWSRF administration from state drinking water administrators and report to Congress on best practices for implementing the DWSRF to facilitate the application process and to improve DWSRF financial management and sustainability." (doc.txt)
[E7] "AWIA makes the most substantial revisions to the DWSRF provisions of SDWA since the program was authorized in 1996. These revisions expand the eligible uses of DWSRF financial assistance, provide states with additional flexibility to administer the DWSRF program, and include provisions intended to make DWSRF assistance more accessible to public water systems." (doc.txt)
</evidence>
<answer>
In doc.txt, all of the described parts of AWIA Section 2015 concern drinking water, because the section amends the Drinking Water State Revolving Fund (DWSRF) provisions of the Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) [E7]. The water-related parts are:

- **Section 2015(a)**: Expressly allows DWSRF funds to be used for projects that replace or rehabilitate aging drinking water treatment, storage, or distribution systems; under EPA guidance such projects were already eligible if needed to protect public health, and they account for 66.1% of the estimated drinking water infrastructure need, but they had not previously been explicitly identified in statute [E1].
- **Section 2015(c)**: Revises DWSRF financial assistance for disadvantaged communities by raising the share of a state's capitalization grant that may be dedicated to additional subsidization from 30% to 35% (while conditionally requiring at least 6% to be used for these subsidies) and extending the amortization period for loans to disadvantaged communities from 30 to 40 years [E2].
- **Section 2015(d)**: Extends the repayment and amortization period for all DWSRF-financed projects: the initial principal and interest payment is due 18 months after project completion instead of within one year, and the amortization period for DWSRF-assisted projects can be extended from 20 to 30 years [E3].
- **Section 2015(e)**: Requires EPA to evaluate and include, to the extent practicable, the cost to replace lead service lines in the drinking water infrastructure needs survey (conducted every four years), which EPA uses to allot the DWSRF appropriation among states and which may affect some states' allotments [E4].
- **Section 2015(f)**: Removes the fiscal-year limitation on source water assessment funding, authorizing states to use a portion of their DWSRF capitalization grant to fund source water assessments or update an existing one [E5].
- **Section 2015(g)**: Requires EPA to gather specified information on DWSRF administration from state drinking water administrators and to report to Congress on best practices for implementing the DWSRF, to facilitate the application process and improve DWSRF financial management and sustainability [E6].

Overall, these revisions expand the eligible uses of DWSRF financial assistance, give states more flexibility in administering the DWSRF program, and make DWSRF assistance more accessible to public water systems [E7].
</answer>
